scenes.text: Health promotion's biggest Australian success is smoking. In nineteen ninety-one, about a quarter of Australians aged fourteen and over smoked daily. In twenty twenty-two to twenty-three, it was about one in twelve. And it didn't happen because people learned smoking was bad. Surveys show most smokers already knew. So write down what actually changed, and for each change, whether it was aimed at the smoker, or at something else.

The World Health Organization defines health promotion as the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health. Control is the key word. A hospital improves health. A campaign that tells people what to do, without changing their circumstances, adds information, not control. So health promotion isn't health care, which treats people who are already unwell, and it isn't just health education. It includes education, but also changes the conditions that decide whether education can be acted on.

Australia has used three approaches, and each asks a different first question. The biomedical approach asks: what's wrong with this body, and how do we fix it? It's the narrow meaning you met at the start, health as no disease, turned into action. The behavioural approach asks: what's this person doing wrong, and how do we get them to stop? The socio-ecological approach asks: what conditions are producing this pattern, and who can change them? They aren't ranked. A broken leg needs the biomedical approach, and no amount of town planning will set it. All three still operate today, nested inside each other.

The first shift, from biomedical to behavioural, came from a change in what was killing people. Early last century, infections dominated, and sanitation, vaccination and antibiotics beat them. By the nineteen seventies, the leading killers were heart disease and cancer, which develop over decades and are linked to smoking, diet, alcohol and inactivity. By the time they show up, much of the damage is done. So attention moved upstream, to behaviours.

The second shift, from behavioural to socio-ecological, came from the inequity data. Education campaigns did work, but unevenly. Rates fell fastest among people who already had the money, time and support to act on the advice. So the average improved while the gap widened, the same pattern we've now seen several times. And the behavioural question produces victim blaming, blaming a person for an outcome their conditions produced. If you first ask what someone's doing wrong, the answer to inequity becomes worse choices, and that gets cause and effect backwards.

Smoking shows all three at once. Biomedical: nicotine replacement and quitting support through doctors. Behavioural: graphic television ads and warnings on packets. Socio-ecological: tax rises that made cigarettes among the most expensive in the world, advertising bans, smoke-free workplaces and venues, and plain packaging from twenty twelve. Most of that list isn't aimed at the smoker at all. A tax rise or a venue ban reaches people no campaign ever reached, because you don't need to have seen anything.

The syllabus names two more. The salutogenic model flips the question: instead of what causes disease, it asks what creates health, like a sense that life is understandable, manageable and meaningful. And Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander approaches see health holistically, as social, emotional, cultural, spiritual and physical wellbeing, connected to community and Country, with communities leading. The sociocultural and ecological models the syllabus lists sit inside the outer band.

Australia built on international agreements. The nineteen seventy-eight Declaration of Alma-Ata made primary health care the basis of Health for All. That's essential, affordable care close to home, including prevention, not just a GP visit. It also said health is made outside hospitals, across many sectors. The Ottawa Charter in nineteen eighty-six turned that into action areas, which is next time. Jakarta in nineteen ninety-seven added partnerships, including with business, and Bangkok in two thousand and five tackled globalisation and marketing. And UNESCO works with the WHO on health-promoting schools.

So what's the nature of health promotion in Australia? It's a system, not a list of campaigns. It's shared across levels of government, and across sectors. It's increasingly aimed at prevention, though prevention is still a small share of health spending. And it's targeted at equity, naming priority groups.
Two things to remember. Information is not control. And each shift was forced by what stopped working.

Two exam questions. First. To cut teenage vaping, a doctor prescribes nicotine replacement, a social media campaign shows the harms, and the government restricts where vapes are sold. Identify each approach, and explain which best reaches young people a campaign misses. Pause here to answer.

The prescription is biomedical, the campaign is behavioural, and the sales restriction is socio-ecological. The restriction is most likely to reach those a campaign misses, because it changes what's available to everyone, whether or not they've seen the message, or have the support to act on it. The classic mistake is calling the campaign health promotion's strongest tool.
Second. Explain the nature of health promotion in Australia, referring to the approaches taken and the global policies that shaped them. Pause here to answer.

Characterise the system: multi-level, multi-sector, aimed at prevention and equity. Then explain why: each approach was displaced by evidence, chronic disease then the widening gap. Tie it to global policy: Alma-Ata's primary health care and work across sectors, Ottawa's action areas, and partnerships from Jakarta. The classic mistake is describing three campaigns instead of a system.

So, for any strategy, ask which question it starts from, who it reaches, and which policy idea it carries. Next, the Ottawa Charter turns the outer band into five action areas, and explains why an outdoor gym nobody uses failed.
